newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Fresh violence as Vranitzky holds Albania talks.
newsitem.headline: Fresh violence as Vranitzky holds Albania talks.

text.p: Fourteen people were injured in explosions at an ammunition dump in southern Albania on Thursday as European envoy Franz Vranitzky met political leaders for last-ditch talks to stop a slide back into chaos.
Military officials and doctors said 14 people were taken to hospital with burns after blasts rocked the dump near Gjirokaster in southern Albania, and six were transferred to a hospital in Greece.
Vranitzky returned to Tirana for the second time in a week to rescue planned elections aimed at restoring political stability to the volatile ex-communist Balkan country.

President Sali Berisha on Wednesday postponed a decree to call the elections for June 29. Most political parties had threatened to boycott the polls because of rules which they saw as biased in favour of Berisha's Democratic Party .
"It was a good meeting," former Austrian chancellor Vranitzky said after talks with Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.

In a reminder of the power-keg situation in the country, shots rang out at one point outside the building where they were meeting. Nervous soldiers fired twice in the air after a car refused to stop at a checkpoint.
Elsewhere, gunmen unleashed a round of bullets in a street of eastern Tirana in what was believed to be a gang fight.
Volleys of gunfire during the night are still common in the capital although shooting during the day has been rare.
In Gjirokaster, officials said explosions at the ammunition dump were continuing. They spoke of a "big dynamite explosion" in underground tunnels and in depots on the surface.
Local residents said the army was removing ammunition, powder and shells from the warehouses when the blast took place.

Ammunition dumps all over Albania were looted during violent unrest which swept the country earlier this year, triggered by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes in which thousands lost their life savings. Two weeks ago a dump exploded in northern Albania, killing 27 people.

Vranitzky, acting on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), had a day of tough talks ahead to find a compromise over the election law and get all parties to take part in the planned vote.
After Fino, he was to see Socialist Party leader Fatos Nano and the head of Berisha's Democratic Party, Tritan Shehu. Talks with Berisha himself were planned later in the day.

Vranitzky's last trip on May 9 ended with a political contract under which the nine main parties agreed to pass a new electoral law and then call a vote for the end of June. To meet the election target date of June 29, Berisha would have to issue a decree on Thursday, 45 days before the planned vote.

Trouble blew up as most of the parties of a nine-party interim Government of National Reconciliation said they would boycott the polls because Berisha's Democratic Party had pushed a law through parliament which gave it an advantage.
The smaller parties, led by the Socialists, want more seats allocated on a proportional basis while the Democratic Party favours more decided by majority vote.
The other parties were also furious the law was presented by the Democrats rather than the unity government.
The Socialists pulled out of the last elections in May 1996, which international observers said were flawed.
